extraction_notes.note: The Zarankiewicz conjecture and Turan's brickyard problem are only named (abstract, introduction), never stated apart from Theorem 1.1, so no conjecture/open_problem node and no resolves edge; the abstract's copy of the formula is in TP1.also_stated_at.

The introduction's proof outline is a proof sketch: the sketch rule asks for rigor semi_formal and an alternative proves edge, while the rigor rule excludes proofs; the specific sketch rule was followed.
Equation (1.2) in the introduction restates Lemma 2.1 (same inequality as (2.1)); treated as a restated copy (LP1.also_stated_at), no node of its own.

(5.1), the upper bound from the classical axis (Zarankiewicz) drawing, is kept an equation inside the proof of Theorem 1.1 though it is a result in its own right, referred to later as 'the upper bound'.

Lemma A.1 kept origin paper although the appendix calls the adjacent-crossing removal 'a standard ordinary-crossing reduction' [FulekEtAl2012]; only that part is attributed, the continuous-arc normalization is the paper's own.

Two TikZ figures sit inside or between proof environments; the figure code is inside PP4's verbatim statement but no step covers it. The proof of Lemma 4.1 follows a figure, so its proves edge to LP4 was set by hand.

nodes.name: plane drawing
nodes.statement: For a finite graph $G$, a plane drawing places its vertices at distinct points and represents each edge by a simple continuous arc whose interior avoids the vertices.
nodes.genus: places its vertices at distinct points
differentia: represents each edge by a simple continuous arc whose interior avoids the vertices

nodes.name: proper crossing
nodes.statement: A meeting of two edge interiors is a proper crossing if some open neighborhood of the point has a homeomorphism onto an open disk taking the point to its center and the two local edge traces onto its horizontal and vertical diameters.
nodes.statement_short: A point where two edge interiors meet is a proper crossing if locally homeomorphic to two crossing diameters of a disk.

nodes.name: admissible drawing
nodes.statement: We require that edge interiors meet at finitely many proper crossings, with no triple crossings, tangencies, or common subarcs.

nodes.name: crossing count c(D)
nodes.statement: The number $c(D)$ of a drawing $D$ counts crossing points: if two edges cross several times, each crossing is counted.
nodes.origin_citation: standard; point-count convention of Pach & Toth 2000, Fulek et al. 2012

nodes.name: ordinary crossing number
nodes.statement: The ordinary crossing number is \[ \mathrm{cr}(G)=\min_D c(D). \]
nodes.origin_citation: standard; point-count convention of Pach & Toth 2000, Fulek et al. 2012

nodes.name: complete bipartite graph K_{m,n}
nodes.statement: Let $K_{m,n}$ be the complete bipartite graph with vertex classes $\{a_1,\ldots,a_m\}$ and $\{b_1,\ldots,b_n\}$.

nodes.name: Zarankiewicz factor d_r
nodes.statement: Put \begin{equation} d_r=\left\lfloor\frac r2\right\rfloor \left\lfloor\frac{r-1}{2}\right\rfloor =\binom{\lfloor r/2\rfloor}{2} +\binom{\lceil r/2\rceil}{2}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $d_r=\lfloor r/2\rfloor\lfloor (r-1)/2\rfloor$, also a sum of two binomials.

nodes.name: definition of d_r
nodes.statement: d_r=\left\lfloor\frac r2\right\rfloor \left\lfloor\frac{r-1}{2}\right\rfloor =\binom{\lfloor r/2\rfloor}{2} +\binom{\lceil r/2\rceil}{2}.
nodes.label: eq:dr

nodes.name: Zarankiewicz crossing-number formula for K_{m,n}
nodes.statement: For all positive integers $m,n$, \[ \mathrm{cr}(K_{m,n})=d_m d_n. \]
also_stated_at: For all positive integers $m,n$, the ordinary crossing number of the complete bipartite graph $K_{m,n}$ is \[ \left\lfloor\frac m2\right\rfloor \left\lfloor\frac{m-1}{2}\right\rfloor \left\lfloor\frac n2\right\rfloor \left\lfloor\frac{n-1}{2}\right\rfloor. \]
nodes.statement_short: The crossing number of $K_{m,n}$ is exactly $d_m d_n$ (Zarankiewicz's conjecture).
nodes.label: thm:main

nodes.name: Kleitman's theorem (min(m,n) <= 6)
nodes.statement: Kleitman established the exact formula when one vertex class has at most six vertices~\cite{Kleitman1970}.
assumptions: when one vertex class has at most six vertices
nodes.statement_short: Zarankiewicz's formula holds when one vertex class has at most six vertices.

nodes.name: Woodall's computation of cr(K_{7,7}) and cr(K_{7,9})
nodes.statement: Woodall developed this approach through cyclic-order graphs and verified the cases $K_{7,7}$ and $K_{7,9}$ by computation~\cite{Woodall1993}.
conclusions: verified the cases $K_{7,7}$ and $K_{7,9}$ by computation

nodes.name: Balogh-Lidicky-Norin-Pfender-Salazar-Spiro flag-algebra bound
nodes.statement: For balanced graphs, Balogh, Lidick\'y, Norin, Pfender, Salazar, and Spiro obtained \[ \operatorname{cr}(K_{n,n})\ge0.9118\,d_n^2+o(n^4) \] using Razborov's flag-algebra method~\cite{Razborov2007,BaloghEtAl2023}.
nodes.origin_citation: Balogh, Lidicky, Norin, Pfender, Salazar, Spiro 2023
nodes.statement_short: Asymptotic lower bound $\mathrm{cr}(K_{n,n})\ge 0.9118 d_n^2+o(n^4)$ via flag algebras.

nodes.name: half comparison-sign matrix S_prec
nodes.statement: For a linear order $\prec$ on $\{1,\ldots,n\}$, let $S_\prec$ be half its comparison-sign matrix: its $(p,q)$ entry is $\tfrac12$ if $p\prec q$, $-\tfrac12$ if $q\prec p$, and $0$ if $p=q$.
differentia: its $(p,q)$ entry is $\tfrac12$ if $p\prec q$, $-\tfrac12$ if $q\prec p$, and $0$ if $p=q$

nodes.name: Proof outline of Theorem 1.1
nodes.statement: To connect these statements, normalize a minimum drawing $D$ so its edges are polygonal and adjacent edges do not cross. Orient edges from the first vertex class to the second. At each vertex, read the counterclockwise spoke order from a chosen gap. Form a matrix $J$ indexed by these edges. Its entry for two distinct edges is their signed crossing count, plus half their comparison sign in the incident order if they share an endpoint; diagonal entries are zero. The block $J^{ik}$ compares the edges incident with $a_i$ to those incident with $a_k$. The vanishing of algebraic intersections of closed plane curves makes these blocks additive modulo row-plus-column terms (Section~\ref{sec:intersections}). Applying the linear map produces the family $X_i-Y_j$: diagonal blocks have full rank, and off-diagonal ranks are bounded by the corresponding crossing counts. Corollary~\ref{cor:rank-sum} bounds the ordered sum of off-diagonal ranks below by $2d_m d_n$. The corresponding sum of crossing counts counts each crossing twice, so the rank sum is at most $2c(D)$. This gives $c(D)\ge d_m d_n$. Section~\ref{sec:formula} completes the proof: deleting vertices gives the even case, and the classical balanced-axis drawing gives the matching upper bound.
nodes.statement_short: Outline: signed-intersection matrix $J$ of a normalized drawing, blocks additive by cycle pairing; the rank detector and the rank-sum corollary give $c(D)\ge d_md_n$.

nodes.name: normalize the drawing and read spoke orders

nodes.statement_short: Normalize a minimum drawing, orient edges, read the spoke order at each vertex.

nodes.name: blocks additive

nodes.statement_short: Blocks are additive modulo row-plus-column terms.

nodes.name: Subspace intersection bound
nodes.statement: Let $W$ be a real vector space of dimension $N$, and let $U_1,\ldots,U_m,V_1,\ldots,V_m$ be subspaces of $W$, where $m\geq1$. If $U_i\cap V_i=\{0\}$ for every $i$, then \begin{equation} \sum_{i,j=1}^{m}\dim(U_i\cap V_j) \leq \left\lfloor\frac{m^2}{4}\right\rfloor N. \end{equation}
also_stated_at: In Section~\ref{sec:subspaces}, we prove that subspaces $U_i,V_i$ of an $N$-dimensional real vector space satisfying $U_i\cap V_i=0$ obey \begin{equation} \sum_{i,j=1}^m\dim(U_i\cap V_j) \le \left\lfloor\frac{m^2}{4}\right\rfloor N. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: If $U_i\cap V_i=0$ for all $i$, then $\sum_{i,j}\dim(U_i\cap V_j)\le\lfloor m^2/4\rfloor N$.
assumptions: Let $W$ be a real vector space of dimension $N$, and let $U_1,\ldots,U_m,V_1,\ldots,V_m$ be subspaces of $W$, where $m\geq1$
nodes.label: lem:subspace

nodes.name: subspace intersection bound (2.1)
nodes.statement: \sum_{i,j=1}^{m}\dim(U_i\cap V_j) \leq \left\lfloor\frac{m^2}{4}\right\rfloor N.
nodes.label: eq:subspace-bound

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.1
nodes.statement:
We encode the subspaces by polynomial evaluation constraints. Evaluating away from the constraint nodes gives a filtration of evaluation spaces. At each node, disjointness bounds the evaluated rank. The resulting rank deficiency gives a lower bound on a polynomial minor's vanishing order. Comparing these orders with the minor's degree, then summing over the filtration, will give the bound. Choose distinct real numbers $t_1,\ldots,t_m$. For a subspace $Z\subseteq W$ and an integer $h\geq0$, define \[ \mathcal P_h(Z)= \{P\in Z[\xi]:\deg P\leq h,\ P(t_i)\in U_i	ext{ for every }i\}, \qquad \mathcal P_{-1}(Z)=\{0\}. \] Here $Z[\xi]$ denotes polynomials whose coefficients belong to $Z$. Write $E_h(Z;t)=\{P(t):P\in\mathcal P_h(Z)\}$ and put \[ k_h(Z)=\dim\mathcal P_h(Z)-\dim\mathcal P_{h-1}(Z), \qquad k_{-1}(Z)=0. \] \emph{Evaluation away from the nodes.} For $t
otin\{t_1,\ldots,t_m\}$, the kernel of evaluation at $t$ is \[ \ker igl(\mathcal P_h(Z)\longrightarrow Z,\ P\longmapsto P(t) igr) =(\xi-t)\mathcal P_{h-1}(Z). \] Indeed, division by $\xi-t$ preserves the coefficient space $Z$, and it preserves each constraint at $t_i$ because $t_i-t
e0$. The converse inclusion follows by multiplication. Therefore  egin{equation} \dim E_h(Z;t)=k_h(Z) \qquad(t
otin\{t_1,\ldots,t_m\}). \end{equation} Also, evaluation at all $m$ nodes is an isomorphism \[ \mathcal P_{m-1}(Z)\longrightarrow  igoplus_{i=1}^{m}(U_i\cap Z). \] Its inverse sends $(z_1,\ldots,z_m)$ to the polynomial $\sum_i L_i(\xi)z_i$, where $L_i(\xi)=\prod_{k
e i}(\xi-t_k)/(t_i-t_k)$. Uniqueness follows because a scalar polynomial of degree at most $m-1$ with $m$ distinct roots vanishes, applied in coordinates of $Z$. Consequently  egin{equation} \sum_{h=0}^{m-1}k_h(Z) =\dim\mathcal P_{m-1}(Z) =\sum_{i=1}^{m}\dim(U_i\cap Z). \end{equation} \emph{Polynomial minors of controlled degree.} Fix $t_*$ outside the nodes. The spaces $E_h(W;t_*)$ are nested, so \[ \ell_h=k_h(W)-k_{h-1}(W)\geq0 \qquad(0\leq h\leq m-1). \] At stage $h$, choose $\ell_h$ polynomials from $\mathcal P_h(W)$ whose values at $t_*$ extend the previously chosen values to a basis of $E_h(W;t_*)$. In fixed coordinates of $W$, let $M_h(\xi)$ be the matrix of all polynomial columns chosen through stage $h$. It has $r_h=k_h(W)$ columns, independent at $t_*$, and hence has an $r_h$-row square minor $\Delta_h(\xi)$ with $\Delta_h(t_*)
e0$. Each column introduced at stage $e$ has degree at most $e$. Expanding the determinant thus gives  egin{equation} \deg\Delta_h\leq\sum_{e=0}^{h}e\ell_e. \end{equation} If $r_h=0$, use the empty determinant $\Delta_h=1$. \emph{Rank loss at the nodes.} For each $j$ we claim that  egin{equation} \dim E_h(W;t_j)\leq k_h(W)-k_h(V_j). \end{equation} Let $\pi_j:W\longrightarrow W/V_j$ be the quotient map. At every non-node $t$, the kernel of $\pi_j$ on $E_h(W;t)$ contains $E_h(V_j;t)$. Equation~\eqref{eq:filtration-evaluation} gives \[ \dim\pi_j(E_h(W;t))\leq k_h(W)-k_h(V_j). \] To pass to $t_j$, take a fixed basis of the polynomial space $\mathcal P_h(W)$, evaluate its members at the variable $\xi$, and project their columns by $\pi_j$. In fixed coordinates this is a polynomial matrix. Every minor larger than the displayed rank bound vanishes at every non-node, an infinite set, and so is the zero polynomial. Its rank at $t_j$ obeys the same bound. But $E_h(W;t_j)\subseteq U_j$, and $\pi_j$ is injective on $U_j$ because $U_j\cap V_j=\{0\}$. This proves \eqref{eq:node-rank}. The chosen columns of $M_h(t_j)$ lie in $E_h(W;t_j)$, and restricting to the rows of a minor cannot increase rank. The square submatrix defining $\Delta_h$ therefore has rank deficiency at least $k_h(V_j)$ at $t_j$. A square polynomial matrix with deficiency at least $q$ at $t_j$ has determinant divisible by $(\xi-t_j)^q$: choose $q$ independent vectors in its kernel at $t_j$, extend them to a constant invertible column change, and observe that the corresponding $q$ transformed columns vanish at $t_j$. Each contributes the factor $\xi-t_j$, while the column change rescales the determinant by a nonzero constant. Applying this observation separately at the distinct nodes shows that \[ \prod_{j=1}^{m}(\xi-t_j)^{k_h(V_j)}\quad	ext{divides }\Delta_h(\xi). \] For $r_h=0$, all $k_h(V_j)$ are zero by \eqref{eq:filtration-evaluation}, so this assertion also holds for the empty determinant. Since $\Delta_h$ is not the zero polynomial, \eqref{eq:minor-degree} now yields  egin{equation} \sum_{j=1}^{m}k_h(V_j)\leq\sum_{e=0}^{h}e\ell_e. \end{equation} \emph{Summing the degree bounds.} Sum \eqref{eq:multiplicity-budget} over $h=0,\ldots,m-1$ and apply \eqref{eq:filtration-sum} with $Z=V_j$. The result is  egin{align*} \sum_{i,j=1}^{m}\dim(U_i\cap V_j) &\leq\sum_{h=0}^{m-1}\sum_{e=0}^{h}e\ell_e =\sum_{e=0}^{m-1}e(m-e)\ell_e\ &\leq\left\lfloor rac{m^2}{4}ightfloor \sum_{e=0}^{m-1}\ell_e \leq\left\lfloor rac{m^2}{4}ightfloor N. \end{align*} The last step uses $\sum_e\ell_e=k_{m-1}(W)=\dim E_{m-1}(W;t_*)\leq N$.
nodes.statement_short: Polynomial interpolation with subspace constraints at nodes $t_i$: a minor of the evaluation matrix vanishes to order $k_h(V_j)$ at each node; comparing with its degree and summing over the filtration gives the bound.

nodes.name: claim (2.5)
nodes.statement: For each $j$ we claim that \begin{equation} \dim E_h(W;t_j)\leq k_h(W)-k_h(V_j). \end{equation} Let $\pi_j:W\longrightarrow W/V_j$ be the quotient map. At every non-node $t$, the kernel of $\pi_j$ on $E_h(W;t)$ contains $E_h(V_j;t)$. Equation~\eqref{eq:filtration-evaluation} gives \[ \dim\pi_j(E_h(W;t))\leq k_h(W)-k_h(V_j). \] To pass to $t_j$, take a fixed basis of the polynomial space $\mathcal P_h(W)$, evaluate its members at the variable $\xi$, and project their columns by $\pi_j$. In fixed coordinates this is a polynomial matrix. Every minor larger than the displayed rank bound vanishes at every non-node, an infinite set, and so is the zero polynomial. Its rank at $t_j$ obeys the same bound. But $E_h(W;t_j)\subseteq U_j$, and $\pi_j$ is injective on $U_j$ because $U_j\cap V_j=\{0\}$. This proves \eqref{eq:node-rank}.
nodes.statement_short: Claim: $\dim E_h(W;t_j)\le k_h(W)-k_h(V_j)$.

nodes.name: quotient bound at non-nodes
nodes.statement: Let $\pi_j:W\longrightarrow W/V_j$ be the quotient map. At every non-node $t$, the kernel of $\pi_j$ on $E_h(W;t)$ contains $E_h(V_j;t)$. Equation~\eqref{eq:filtration-evaluation} gives \[ \dim\pi_j(E_h(W;t))\leq k_h(W)-k_h(V_j). \]
nodes.statement_short: Project by $W\to W/V_j$; bound the image at non-nodes.

nodes.name: pass to the node
nodes.statement: To pass to $t_j$, take a fixed basis of the polynomial space $\mathcal P_h(W)$, evaluate its members at the variable $\xi$, and project their columns by $\pi_j$. In fixed coordinates this is a polynomial matrix. Every minor larger than the displayed rank bound vanishes at every non-node, an infinite set, and so is the zero polynomial. Its rank at $t_j$ obeys the same bound.
nodes.statement_short: Minors vanishing at infinitely many points vanish identically, so the bound holds at $t_j$.

nodes.name: injectivity on U_j
nodes.statement: But $E_h(W;t_j)\subseteq U_j$, and $\pi_j$ is injective on $U_j$ because $U_j\cap V_j=\{0\}$. This proves \eqref{eq:node-rank}.
nodes.statement_short: $\pi_j$ is injective on $U_j$ since $U_j\cap V_j=0$.

nodes.name: rank deficiency of the minor
nodes.statement: The chosen columns of $M_h(t_j)$ lie in $E_h(W;t_j)$, and restricting to the rows of a minor cannot increase rank. The square submatrix defining $\Delta_h$ therefore has rank deficiency at least $k_h(V_j)$ at $t_j$.
nodes.statement_short: The minor's submatrix has deficiency $\ge k_h(V_j)$ at $t_j$.

nodes.name: vanishing order
nodes.statement: A square polynomial matrix with deficiency at least $q$ at $t_j$ has determinant divisible by $(\xi-t_j)^q$: choose $q$ independent vectors in its kernel at $t_j$, extend them to a constant invertible column change, and observe that the corresponding $q$ transformed columns vanish at $t_j$. Each contributes the factor $\xi-t_j$, while the column change rescales the determinant by a nonzero constant. Applying this observation separately at the distinct nodes shows that \[ \prod_{j=1}^{m}(\xi-t_j)^{k_h(V_j)}\quad\text{divides }\Delta_h(\xi). \]
nodes.statement_short: Rank deficiency $q$ at $t_j$ gives a factor $(\xi-t_j)^q$ of the determinant.

nodes.name: multiplicity budget
nodes.statement: For $r_h=0$, all $k_h(V_j)$ are zero by \eqref{eq:filtration-evaluation}, so this assertion also holds for the empty determinant. Since $\Delta_h$ is not the zero polynomial, \eqref{eq:minor-degree} now yields \begin{equation} \sum_{j=1}^{m}k_h(V_j)\leq\sum_{e=0}^{h}e\ell_e. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Compare vanishing order with degree: (2.6).

nodes.name: Summing the degree bounds
nodes.statement: \emph{Summing the degree bounds.} Sum \eqref{eq:multiplicity-budget} over $h=0,\ldots,m-1$ and apply \eqref{eq:filtration-sum} with $Z=V_j$. The result is \begin{align*} \sum_{i,j=1}^{m}\dim(U_i\cap V_j) &\leq\sum_{h=0}^{m-1}\sum_{e=0}^{h}e\ell_e =\sum_{e=0}^{m-1}e(m-e)\ell_e\\ &\leq\left\lfloor\frac{m^2}{4}\right\rfloor \sum_{e=0}^{m-1}\ell_e \leq\left\lfloor\frac{m^2}{4}\right\rfloor N. \end{align*} The last step uses $\sum_e\ell_e=k_{m-1}(W)=\dim E_{m-1}(W;t_*)\leq N$.
nodes.statement_short: Sum (2.6) over $h$, use (2.3) and $e(m-e)\le\lfloor m^2/4\rfloor$.

nodes.name: evaluation dimension away from nodes (2.2)
nodes.statement: \dim E_h(Z;t)=k_h(Z) \qquad(t\notin\{t_1,\ldots,t_m\}).
nodes.label: eq:filtration-evaluation

nodes.name: filtration sum identity (2.3)
nodes.statement: \sum_{h=0}^{m-1}k_h(Z) =\dim\mathcal P_{m-1}(Z) =\sum_{i=1}^{m}\dim(U_i\cap Z).
nodes.label: eq:filtration-sum

nodes.name: degree bound for the minor (2.4)
nodes.statement: \deg\Delta_h\leq\sum_{e=0}^{h}e\ell_e.
nodes.label: eq:minor-degree

nodes.name: rank bound at the nodes (2.5)
nodes.statement: \dim E_h(W;t_j)\leq k_h(W)-k_h(V_j).
nodes.label: eq:node-rank

nodes.name: multiplicity budget (2.6)
nodes.statement: \sum_{j=1}^{m}k_h(V_j)\leq\sum_{e=0}^{h}e\ell_e.
nodes.label: eq:multiplicity-budget

nodes.name: Sharpness of the subspace intersection bound
nodes.statement: The constant in Lemma~\ref{lem:subspace} is sharp. Write $W=P\oplus Q$ and divide the indices into groups of sizes $a=\lfloor m/2\rfloor$ and $b=\lceil m/2\rceil$. Set $(U_i,V_i)=(P,Q)$ in the first group and $(U_i,V_i)=(Q,P)$ in the second. Only pairs from different groups contribute, and their total is $ab(\dim P+\dim Q)=\lfloor m^2/4\rfloor N$.
nodes.statement_short: Splitting $W=P\oplus Q$ and the indices into two halves attains $\lfloor m^2/4\rfloor N$.

nodes.name: Rank sum for differences
nodes.statement: Let $X_1,\ldots,X_m,Y_1,\ldots,Y_m$ be real $d\times d$ matrices. If $X_i-Y_i$ is invertible for every $i$, then \begin{equation} \sum_{\substack{1\leq i,j\leq m\\i\ne j}} \mathrm{rank}(X_i-Y_j)\geq2d_m d, \qquad d_m=\left\lfloor\frac m2\right\rfloor \left\lfloor\frac{m-1}{2}\right\rfloor. \end{equation} The sum is over ordered pairs of distinct indices.
nodes.statement_short: If every $X_i-Y_i$ is invertible ($d\times d$), then $\sum_{i\ne j}\mathrm{rank}(X_i-Y_j)\ge 2d_m d$.
conclusions: \begin{equation} \sum_{\substack{1\leq i,j\leq m\\i\ne j}} \mathrm{rank}(X_i-Y_j)\geq2d_m d, \qquad d_m=\left\lfloor\frac m2\right\rfloor \left\lfloor\frac{m-1}{2}\right\rfloor. \end{equation}
The sum is over ordered pairs of distinct indices.
nodes.label: cor:rank-sum

nodes.name: rank sum inequality (2.7)
nodes.statement: \sum_{\substack{1\leq i,j\leq m\\i\ne j}} \mathrm{rank}(X_i-Y_j)\geq2d_m d, \qquad d_m=\left\lfloor\frac m2\right\rfloor \left\lfloor\frac{m-1}{2}\right\rfloor.
nodes.label: eq:rank-sum

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 2.3
nodes.statement: In $W=\mathbb R^d\oplus\mathbb R^d$, let \[ U_i=\{(v,X_iv):v\in\mathbb R^d\},\qquad V_j=\{(v,Y_jv):v\in\mathbb R^d\}. \] The map $v\mapsto(v,X_iv)$ identifies $\ker(X_i-Y_j)$ with $U_i\cap V_j$. Thus \[ \dim(U_i\cap V_j)=d-\mathrm{rank}(X_i-Y_j), \qquad U_i\cap V_i=\{0\}. \] Lemma~\ref{lem:subspace}, with $N=2d$, gives \[ \sum_{i,j=1}^{m}\mathrm{rank}(X_i-Y_j) \geq\left(m^2-2\left\lfloor\frac{m^2}{4}\right\rfloor\right)d. \] The $m$ diagonal terms each equal $d$. Removing them gives \eqref{eq:rank-sum}, because \[ m^2-m-2\left\lfloor\frac{m^2}{4}\right\rfloor =\begin{cases} 2r(r-1),&m=2r,\\ 2r^2,&m=2r+1, \end{cases} =2d_m. \]
nodes.statement_short: Apply Lemma 2.1 to the graphs of $X_i$ and $Y_j$ in $\mathbb R^d\oplus\mathbb R^d$ and remove the diagonal terms.

nodes.name: graphs of linear maps
nodes.statement: In $W=\mathbb R^d\oplus\mathbb R^d$, let \[ U_i=\{(v,X_iv):v\in\mathbb R^d\},\qquad V_j=\{(v,Y_jv):v\in\mathbb R^d\}. \] The map $v\mapsto(v,X_iv)$ identifies $\ker(X_i-Y_j)$ with $U_i\cap V_j$. Thus \[ \dim(U_i\cap V_j)=d-\mathrm{rank}(X_i-Y_j), \qquad U_i\cap V_i=\{0\}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Take graph subspaces; $\dim(U_i\cap V_j)=d-\mathrm{rank}(X_i-Y_j)$.

nodes.name: apply Lemma 2.1
nodes.statement: Lemma~\ref{lem:subspace}, with $N=2d$, gives \[ \sum_{i,j=1}^{m}\mathrm{rank}(X_i-Y_j) \geq\left(m^2-2\left\lfloor\frac{m^2}{4}\right\rfloor\right)d. \]
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 2.1 with $N=2d$ bounds the full rank sum below.

nodes.name: remove diagonal
nodes.statement: The $m$ diagonal terms each equal $d$. Removing them gives \eqref{eq:rank-sum}, because \[ m^2-m-2\left\lfloor\frac{m^2}{4}\right\rfloor =\begin{cases} 2r(r-1),&m=2r,\\ 2r^2,&m=2r+1, \end{cases} =2d_m. \]
nodes.statement_short: Subtract the $m$ diagonal terms; arithmetic gives $2d_m$.

nodes.name: normalized minimum drawing D
nodes.statement: Fix a minimum drawing $D$ of $K_{m,n}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:normalization}, proved in Appendix~\ref{sec:normalization}, we may take its edges to be polygonal, straight in a neighborhood of every crossing and vertex, with no crossings between edges having a common endpoint.
nodes.statement_short: Fix a minimum drawing, normalized (polygonal, locally straight, no adjacent-edge crossings).

nodes.name: orientation of edge ip
nodes.statement: Orient the edge $ip$ from $a_i$ to $b_p$.

nodes.name: signed intersection I(e,f)
nodes.statement: For oriented edges $e,f$, let $I(e,f)$ be the sum of the signs of their interior crossings.
nodes.genus: the sum of the signs of their interior crossings

nodes.name: positive crossing
nodes.statement: A crossing is positive when the ordered directions of $e$ and $f$ give the positive orientation of the plane.

nodes.name: I(e,e)=0 convention
nodes.statement: Set $I(e,e)=0$.

nodes.name: counterclockwise spoke order at a vertex
nodes.statement: At a vertex $v$, choose a gap between consecutive outward spokes and list the incident edges counterclockwise from that gap.

nodes.name: order sign T_v and orientation sign sigma
nodes.statement: Define \[ T_v(e,f)= \begin{cases} 1,&e\text{ precedes }f,\\ -1,&f\text{ precedes }e,\\ 0,&e=f, \end{cases} \qquad \sigma_{ve}= \begin{cases} 1,&e\text{ is oriented out of }v,\\ -1,&e\text{ is oriented into }v. \end{cases} \]
nodes.statement_short: $T_v(e,f)=\pm1$ by which edge precedes in the spoke order; $\sigma_{ve}=\pm1$ by whether $e$ leaves or enters $v$.

nodes.name: signed-intersection matrix J
nodes.statement: The matrix indexed by the edges that we use is \begin{equation} J(e,f)=I(e,f)+\frac12 \sum_{\substack{v\text{ an endpoint}\\\text{of both }e,f}} \sigma_{ve}\sigma_{vf}T_v(e,f), \qquad J^{ik}(p,q)=J(ip,kq). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $J(e,f)$ = signed crossing count plus half the signed order term at each common endpoint; $J^{ik}$ its $n\times n$ blocks.

nodes.name: signed-intersection matrix (3.1)
nodes.statement: J(e,f)=I(e,f)+\frac12 \sum_{\substack{v\text{ an endpoint}\\\text{of both }e,f}} \sigma_{ve}\sigma_{vf}T_v(e,f), \qquad J^{ik}(p,q)=J(ip,kq).
nodes.label: eq:signed-J

nodes.name: Cycle pairing
nodes.statement: Let $z,y\in\mathbb R^{E(K_{m,n})}$ be the signed edge vectors of two oriented simple graph cycles: an entry is $1$ or $-1$ according as the traversal agrees or disagrees with the fixed edge orientation, and is $0$ on an unused edge. Then \begin{equation} z^{\mathsf T}Jy=0. \end{equation} The cycles may share vertices and edges, and may traverse a shared edge in opposite directions.
nodes.statement_short: For signed edge vectors $z,y$ of any two oriented cycles of $K_{m,n}$, $z^{\mathsf T}Jy=0$.
assumptions: Let $z,y\in\mathbb R^{E(K_{m,n})}$ be the signed edge vectors of two oriented simple graph cycles: an entry is $1$ or $-1$ according as the traversal agrees or disagrees with the fixed edge orientation, and is $0$ on an unused edge
The cycles may share vertices and edges, and may traverse a shared edge in opposite directions.
nodes.label: lem:cycle-pairing

nodes.name: cycle pairing identity (3.2)
nodes.statement: z^{\mathsf T}Jy=0.
nodes.label: eq:cycle-pairing

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.1
nodes.statement_short: Local chord formula (3.3) explains the half-order term; replace one cycle by a closed walk and the other by left/right shifts, then the total signed intersection of two closed plane walks is zero (coning argument). Averaging the two shifts makes shared spokes cancel.

nodes.name: local chord formula
nodes.statement: We first establish the local formula that explains the factor $1/2$. Let $C$ and $E$ be oriented chords of a round disk, with four distinct boundary endpoints. Give each chord's start coefficient $-1$ and its end coefficient $+1$; write these coefficients as $\epsilon_C(u)$ and $\epsilon_E(w)$. For a cut in the boundary away from the endpoints, let $T(u,w)$ be $1$ if $u$ precedes $w$ counterclockwise from the cut, and $-1$ otherwise. Their signed intersection is \begin{equation} I(C,E)=\frac12\sum_{u\in\partial C}\sum_{w\in\partial E} \epsilon_C(u)\epsilon_E(w)T(u,w). \end{equation} Moving the cut past one endpoint changes the right-hand side by a multiple of the sum of the other chord's endpoint coefficients, which is zero. We may therefore cut just before the start of $C$. The right-hand side then becomes \[ -\sum_{\substack{w\text{ on the open counterclockwise arc}\\ \text{from the start to the end of }C}} \epsilon_E(w). \] That boundary arc is on the right of the directed chord $C$. The sum is zero for nonalternating endpoints; for alternating endpoints it is $+1$ when $E$ runs from right to left across $C$, and $-1$ in the reverse case. These are exactly the signed intersection values.
nodes.statement_short: Prove the chord formula (3.3) for signed intersection of two disk chords.

nodes.name: chords and formula
nodes.statement: Let $C$ and $E$ be oriented chords of a round disk, with four distinct boundary endpoints. Give each chord's start coefficient $-1$ and its end coefficient $+1$; write these coefficients as $\epsilon_C(u)$ and $\epsilon_E(w)$. For a cut in the boundary away from the endpoints, let $T(u,w)$ be $1$ if $u$ precedes $w$ counterclockwise from the cut, and $-1$ otherwise. Their signed intersection is \begin{equation} I(C,E)=\frac12\sum_{u\in\partial C}\sum_{w\in\partial E} \epsilon_C(u)\epsilon_E(w)T(u,w). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Set up two oriented chords, endpoint coefficients and boundary order; state (3.3).

nodes.name: cut independence
nodes.statement: Moving the cut past one endpoint changes the right-hand side by a multiple of the sum of the other chord's endpoint coefficients, which is zero. We may therefore cut just before the start of $C$.
nodes.statement_short: The right side is independent of the cut; cut before the start of $C$.

nodes.name: evaluate
nodes.statement: The right-hand side then becomes \[ -\sum_{\substack{w\text{ on the open counterclockwise arc}\\ \text{from the start to the end of }C}} \epsilon_E(w). \] That boundary arc is on the right of the directed chord $C$. The sum is zero for nonalternating endpoints; for alternating endpoints it is $+1$ when $E$ runs from right to left across $C$, and $-1$ in the reverse case. These are exactly the signed intersection values.
nodes.statement_short: The sum counts the other chord's endpoints on the right arc: the signed intersection.

nodes.name: figure pointer
nodes.statement: Figure~\ref{fig:chord-pairing} illustrates the local signs and the averaging at a shared spoke used below.
nodes.statement_short: Figure 1 illustrates the local signs.

nodes.name: first cycle as closed walk gamma
nodes.statement: Choose small pairwise disjoint round vertex disks meeting the drawing only in its straight spokes. Replace the passage of the first cycle through each of its vertex disks by the chord joining its incoming and outgoing boundary points. Outside these disks, keep its original edge tracks. This gives a closed polygonal walk $\gamma$; its drawing may have self-intersections.
nodes.statement_short: Replace the first cycle's vertex passages by chords: closed walk $\gamma$.

nodes.name: shifted walks eta_+-
nodes.statement: For the second cycle construct two closed polygonal walks $\eta_+$ and $\eta_-$ by shifting its edge tracks a small distance to the left and to the right, respectively, relative to the \emph{fixed graph-edge orientation}. In each vertex disk join the shifted boundary endpoints by a chord. Here is an explicit construction of the tracks outside the vertex disks. Place further pairwise disjoint small disks at crossings and nonstraight bends, each meeting only the straight pieces incident with its center. Shift each straight stretch between disks parallel to itself. In a crossing disk continue along the shifted line: it avoids its own original line and meets the other original line once, with the same crossing sign. In a bend disk the two shifted ends lie in the same component of the disk minus the original bent arc, and can be joined there by a polygonal arc. Indeed, for the left shift, the incoming boundary ray moves clockwise and the outgoing ray counterclockwise; both displaced ends are in the sector on the left of the oriented bend. The right shift uses the other sector. All remaining distinct truncated straight stretches are compact and disjoint, so sufficiently small shifts introduce no additional intersections. Finiteness permits one choice of shift size for the entire construction. At vertex-circle seams the two walks' boundary endpoints are distinct and chord interiors lie in the open disk; at crossing disks the intended intersections remain strictly interior. Together with the avoidance inside bend disks, this excludes contacts at seams and corners.
nodes.statement_short: Construct left/right shifted closed walks $\eta_\pm$ of the second cycle.

nodes.name: define shifts
nodes.statement: For the second cycle construct two closed polygonal walks $\eta_+$ and $\eta_-$ by shifting its edge tracks a small distance to the left and to the right, respectively, relative to the \emph{fixed graph-edge orientation}. In each vertex disk join the shifted boundary endpoints by a chord.
nodes.statement_short: Shift edge tracks left and right; join by chords in vertex disks.

nodes.name: explicit tracks
nodes.statement: Here is an explicit construction of the tracks outside the vertex disks. Place further pairwise disjoint small disks at crossings and nonstraight bends, each meeting only the straight pieces incident with its center. Shift each straight stretch between disks parallel to itself. In a crossing disk continue along the shifted line: it avoids its own original line and meets the other original line once, with the same crossing sign. In a bend disk the two shifted ends lie in the same component of the disk minus the original bent arc, and can be joined there by a polygonal arc. Indeed, for the left shift, the incoming boundary ray moves clockwise and the outgoing ray counterclockwise; both displaced ends are in the sector on the left of the oriented bend. The right shift uses the other sector.
nodes.statement_short: Explicit shifted tracks through crossing and bend disks.

nodes.name: no extra intersections
nodes.statement: All remaining distinct truncated straight stretches are compact and disjoint, so sufficiently small shifts introduce no additional intersections. Finiteness permits one choice of shift size for the entire construction.
nodes.statement_short: Small enough shifts add no intersections.

nodes.name: seams and corners
nodes.statement: At vertex-circle seams the two walks' boundary endpoints are distinct and chord interiors lie in the open disk; at crossing disks the intended intersections remain strictly interior. Together with the avoidance inside bend disks, this excludes contacts at seams and corners.
nodes.statement_short: No contacts at seams or corners.

nodes.name: exterior contribution
nodes.statement: Consequently, in each version the signed intersections with $\gamma$ outside the vertex disks sum to \begin{equation} \sum_{e,f}z_e y_f I(e,f)=z^{\mathsf T}Iy. \end{equation} This also describes shared tracks: a shifted edge avoids its own unshifted copy. If both cycles use both edges of an original crossing, the intersections of each shifted track with the other unshifted track give the two ordered-edge contributions in the displayed sum. Their signs include the traversal coefficients $z_e y_f$.
nodes.statement_short: Outside vertex disks the signed intersections sum to $z^{\mathsf T}Iy$ (3.4).

nodes.name: vertex disk contribution
nodes.statement: Consider a vertex disk used by both cycles. The endpoint coefficient of its first chord on spoke $e$ is $\sigma_{ve}z_e$: an incoming traversal starts the chord and an outgoing traversal ends it. The second chord's corresponding coefficient is $\sigma_{vf}y_f$. All endpoints belonging to the two different chords are distinct after either shift. Choose the shifts small enough that the original boundary cut stays in its chosen gap. For different spokes $e,f$, the comparison sign of their endpoints is $T_v(e,f)$ in both versions. For the same spoke, the two shifted endpoints lie on opposite sides of the unshifted endpoint in the boundary order. Their comparison signs therefore average to zero, as required by $T_v(e,e)=0$. Applying \eqref{eq:chord-formula} and averaging, the contribution of this disk is \[ \frac12\sum_{e,f\text{ incident with }v} z_e y_f\sigma_{ve}\sigma_{vf}T_v(e,f). \] This cancellation for a shared spoke is unaffected by opposite cycle traversals: they change the endpoint coefficients, while the two order signs remain opposite.
nodes.statement_short: Each shared vertex disk contributes the half-order term of $J$.

nodes.name: endpoint coefficients
nodes.statement: Consider a vertex disk used by both cycles. The endpoint coefficient of its first chord on spoke $e$ is $\sigma_{ve}z_e$: an incoming traversal starts the chord and an outgoing traversal ends it. The second chord's corresponding coefficient is $\sigma_{vf}y_f$.
nodes.statement_short: Chord endpoint coefficients are $\sigma_{ve}z_e$ and $\sigma_{vf}y_f$.

nodes.name: comparison signs
nodes.statement: All endpoints belonging to the two different chords are distinct after either shift. Choose the shifts small enough that the original boundary cut stays in its chosen gap. For different spokes $e,f$, the comparison sign of their endpoints is $T_v(e,f)$ in both versions. For the same spoke, the two shifted endpoints lie on opposite sides of the unshifted endpoint in the boundary order. Their comparison signs therefore average to zero, as required by $T_v(e,e)=0$.
nodes.statement_short: Different spokes compare by $T_v$; a shared spoke's two signs average to 0.

nodes.name: apply chord formula
nodes.statement: Applying \eqref{eq:chord-formula} and averaging, the contribution of this disk is \[ \frac12\sum_{e,f\text{ incident with }v} z_e y_f\sigma_{ve}\sigma_{vf}T_v(e,f). \]
nodes.statement_short: Chord formula averaged over both shifts gives the local term.

nodes.name: opposite traversals
nodes.statement: This cancellation for a shared spoke is unaffected by opposite cycle traversals: they change the endpoint coefficients, while the two order signs remain opposite.
nodes.statement_short: Opposite traversals do not affect the cancellation.

nodes.name: reduction to zero total
nodes.statement: It remains to show that the total signed intersection of each pair $(\gamma,\eta_\pm)$ is zero.
nodes.statement_short: Remains: total signed intersection of $\gamma$ with $\eta_\pm$ is zero.

nodes.name: closed walks have zero total intersection
nodes.statement: More generally, let two closed polygonal walks meet transversely away from their corners, counting intersections by their segment traversals. Cone every oriented segment $[u,w]$ of the first walk to a point $o$, using the oriented triangle $[o,u,w]$. Choose $o$ outside the finitely many lines that would make a triangle degenerate or a cone segment pass through a corner of the second walk; also avoid its segment lines. The added cone segments meet the second walk transversely away from corners. Each triangle boundary has total signed intersection zero with the second walk: every entrance into the triangle is paired, along that closed walk, with an exit, and the two have opposite signs. On summing triangle boundaries, the extra oriented cone segments cancel in pairs, leaving exactly the first walk. Its total signed intersection with the second is therefore zero. The argument counts traversals and does not require either walk to be simple. The constructed pairs satisfy these transversality conditions; any unnecessary straight subdivision points can be removed.
nodes.statement_short: Cone each segment of one walk to a point; triangle boundaries have zero intersection with a closed walk.

nodes.name: cone construction
nodes.statement: More generally, let two closed polygonal walks meet transversely away from their corners, counting intersections by their segment traversals. Cone every oriented segment $[u,w]$ of the first walk to a point $o$, using the oriented triangle $[o,u,w]$. Choose $o$ outside the finitely many lines that would make a triangle degenerate or a cone segment pass through a corner of the second walk; also avoid its segment lines.
nodes.statement_short: Cone every segment of the first walk to a generic point $o$.

nodes.name: triangles contribute zero
nodes.statement: The added cone segments meet the second walk transversely away from corners. Each triangle boundary has total signed intersection zero with the second walk: every entrance into the triangle is paired, along that closed walk, with an exit, and the two have opposite signs.
nodes.statement_short: Each triangle boundary meets a closed walk with total sign zero.

nodes.name: sum triangles
nodes.statement: On summing triangle boundaries, the extra oriented cone segments cancel in pairs, leaving exactly the first walk. Its total signed intersection with the second is therefore zero. The argument counts traversals and does not require either walk to be simple. The constructed pairs satisfy these transversality conditions; any unnecessary straight subdivision points can be removed.
nodes.statement_short: Cone segments cancel; the walk's total is zero.

nodes.name: conclude
nodes.statement: Finally, average the zero total for $\eta_+$ and $\eta_-$. The exterior contribution is \eqref{eq:exterior-intersections}, and the vertex-disk contributions are exactly the local terms of \eqref{eq:signed-J}. Their sum is $z^{\mathsf T}Jy$, proving \eqref{eq:cycle-pairing}.
nodes.statement_short: Average over $\eta_\pm$: exterior plus vertex terms equal $z^{\mathsf T}Jy=0$.

nodes.name: chord formula (3.3)
nodes.statement: I(C,E)=\frac12\sum_{u\in\partial C}\sum_{w\in\partial E} \epsilon_C(u)\epsilon_E(w)T(u,w).
nodes.label: eq:chord-formula

nodes.name: exterior intersections (3.4)
nodes.statement: \sum_{e,f}z_e y_f I(e,f)=z^{\mathsf T}Iy.
nodes.label: eq:exterior-intersections

nodes.name: additive matrix space L
nodes.statement: Let \begin{equation} \mathcal L=\bigl\{H\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}: H(p,q)=r_p+c_q\text{ for some }r,c\in\mathbb R^n\bigr\}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.1
nodes.statement: The polynomial space has dimension $s^2$, and \[ |Q_s|=\frac{s(s+1)}2+\frac{s(s-1)}2=s^2. \] It therefore suffices to show that a polynomial $P(u,v)$ of degree at most $s-1$ in each variable, vanishing at all these points, is zero. We prove this by induction on $s$. For $s=1$, $P$ is constant and vanishes at the single point indexed by $(2,1)$. Let $s>1$. The first triangle contains the $s$ points $(x_{s+1},x_q)$ for $1\leq q\leq s$. The polynomial $P(x_{s+1},v)$ has degree at most $s-1$ and $s$ distinct roots, so it vanishes identically. Division in the variable $u$ gives \[ P(u,v)=(u-x_{s+1})P_1(u,v), \qquad \deg_u P_1\leq s-2,\quad\deg_v P_1\leq s-1. \] For $p=2,\ldots,s$, the remaining points $(x_p,x_1)$ give $P_1(x_p,x_1)=0$, since $x_p\ne x_{s+1}$. Thus $P_1(u,x_1)$, of degree at most $s-2$, has $s-1$ distinct roots and vanishes identically. Factoring in the second variable, we obtain \begin{equation} P(u,v)=(u-x_{s+1})(v-x_1)R(u,v), \qquad \deg_u R,\deg_v R\leq s-2. \end{equation} At every point in the two remaining triangles the displayed factors are nonzero. Hence \[ R(x_p,x_q)=0 \quad\text{if }2\leq q<p\leq s \quad\text{or if }s+2\leq p<q\leq2s+1. \] Define a tuple of $2s-1$ distinct nodes and a polynomial by \[ (y_1,\ldots,y_{2s-1}) =(x_{s+2},\ldots,x_{2s+1},x_2,\ldots,x_s), \qquad S(u,v)=R(v,u). \] The lower triangle $q<p\leq s$ for the $y$-tuple becomes the remaining upper triangle for the $x$-tuple after the coordinate swap. The upper triangle $s<p<q\leq2s-1$ becomes the remaining lower triangle. Consequently $S$ vanishes at every point of the pattern $Q_{s-1}$ for the $y$-tuple. The induction hypothesis gives $S=0$, hence $R=0$ and $P=0$. This proves injectivity of the square evaluation map and thus both assertions.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.2
nodes.statement:
Set  egin{equation}  egin{gathered} F(t)=\prod_{p=1}^{n}(t-x_p),\qquad h_{pq}=(x_p^a x_q^b)_{0\leq a,b<s},\ B_{pq}= rac{x_p-x_q}{F'(x_p)F'(x_q)} h_{pq}h_{pq}^{\mathsf T},\qquad \Phi(H)=\sum_{p,q=1}^{n}H(p,q)B_{pq}. \end{gathered} \end{equation} The factors $1/F'(x_p)$ are the classical barycentric weights for Lagrange interpolation~\cite[Section~3, equation~(3.2)]{BerrutTrefethen2004}. All denominators are nonzero because the nodes are distinct. The constant coordinate of $h_{pq}$ is $1$, so $B_{pq}$ has rank one when $p
e q$, while $B_{pp}=0$. This proves 	extup{(ii)} and the annihilation of diagonal matrices. Rank subadditivity also gives  egin{equation} \mathrm{rank}\Phi(H)\leq  igl|\{(p,q):p
e q,\ H(p,q)
e0\} igr|. \end{equation} For the additive matrices, we use the elementary identity  egin{equation} \sum_{p=1}^{n} rac{A(x_p)}{F'(x_p)}=0 \qquad	ext{if }\deg A\leq n-2. \end{equation} Indeed, the polynomials $F(t)/((t-x_p)F'(x_p))$ have degree $n-1$ and take the coordinate values $1$ at $x_p$ and $0$ at every other node. Subtracting their linear combination with coefficients $A(x_p)$ from $A$ gives a polynomial of degree at most $n-1$ with $n$ distinct roots, so \[ A(t)=\sum_{p=1}^{n} A(x_p) rac{F(t)}{(t-x_p)F'(x_p)}. \] Comparison of the coefficients of $t^{n-1}$ proves \eqref{eq:lagrange-vanishing}. The entry of $B_{pq}$ indexed by $(a,b)$ and $(a',b')$ is \[  rac{(x_p-x_q)x_p^{a+a'}x_q^{b+b'}} {F'(x_p)F'(x_q)}. \] Its numerator has degree at most $2s-1=n-2$ in either variable separately. Applying \eqref{eq:lagrange-vanishing} with the other variable fixed proves \[ \sum_{q=1}^{n}B_{pq}=0\quad	ext{for every }p, \qquad \sum_{p=1}^{n}B_{pq}=0\quad	ext{for every }q. \] It follows that $\Phi((r_p+c_q)_{p,q})=0$, completing 	extup{(i)}. It remains to prove 	extup{(iii)}. First take the natural order and write $S=S_\prec$. Let $H(p,q)=\mathbf{1}_{q<p}$ and let $\mathbf1$ denote the all-ones column vector. Then \[ S=	frac12\mathbf1\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}-H-	frac12I_n, \qquad \Phi(S)=-\Phi(H). \] Subtract $1$ from each row of $H$ indexed by $p>s+1$, obtaining $H'$. The difference $H-H'$ is additive, so $\Phi(H')=\Phi(H)$. Apart from diagonal entries, which $\Phi$ annihilates, the support of $H'$ is exactly $Q_s$: its value is $+1$ on the first triangle of \eqref{eq:triangular-pattern} and $-1$ on the second. List the pairs in $Q_s$ in any order, and let $A_Q$ be the square matrix with columns $h_{pq}$ in that order. By Lemma~ef{lem:triangular-basis}, $A_Q$ is invertible. Equation \eqref{eq:detector-definition} now gives  egin{equation} \Phi(S)=-A_Q D_Q A_Q^{\mathsf T},\qquad D_Q=\mathrm{diag}\left( H'(p,q) rac{x_p-x_q}{F'(x_p)F'(x_q)} ight)_{(p,q)\in Q_s}. \end{equation} Every diagonal entry of $D_Q$ is nonzero, so $\Phi(S)$ is invertible. Finally let $\pi(1)\prec\cdots\prec\pi(n)$ be an arbitrary order. Relabel the indices and use the tuple $(x_{\pi(1)},\ldots,x_{\pi(n)})$ in the argument just given. The relabeled evaluation vector at $(r,q)$ is $h_{\pi(r),\pi(q)}$, so this only reindexes the sum defining $\Phi(S_\prec)$; the polynomial $F$ and the fixed map $\Phi$ are unchanged. The relabeled nodes are distinct, so Lemma~ef{lem:triangular-basis} applies again. Thus every order has invertible image under the original map.

We now combine the preceding results to prove Theorem~ef{thm:main}. \subsection{The upper bound} We recall the classical axis construction; see Woodall~\cite[p.~658]{Woodall1993}. Place the vertices $a_i$ on the vertical axis, divided as evenly as possible between its positive and negative rays. Place the vertices $b_p$ on the horizontal axis in the same way, and join every required pair by a straight segment. All positions are distinct and nonzero. An edge interior is contained in one open quadrant. In a quadrant whose bounding rays contain $u$ first-class and $v$ second-class vertices, each choice of two vertices on each ray forms a convex quadrilateral. Exactly its diagonals cross, so the contribution is $ inom u2 inom v2$. Summing over the quadrants and using \eqref{eq:dr} gives exactly $d_m d_n$ crossings, provided no three segments concur in their interiors. The positions can be chosen to ensure this condition. Three segments concurrent in their interiors must have six distinct endpoints, since segments with a common endpoint do not cross elsewhere. Their concurrence is a proper polynomial condition on their axis intercepts: keeping two segments fixed and varying an intercept of the third avoids their intersection. There are only finitely many triples, and the product of their nonzero defining polynomials cannot vanish on the open set of permitted positions. Thus an admissible drawing achieves the stated count. In particular,  egin{equation} \mathrm{cr}(K_{m,n})\le d_m d_n. \end{equation} If $m\le2$ or $n\le2$, this already proves equality by nonnegativity. \subsection{The lower bound for odd 	exorpdfstring{$n$}{n}} Assume $m\ge3$ and $n=2s+1\ge3$, and put $d=s^2=d_n$. Choose a minimum drawing $D$ normalized as in Lemma~ef{lem:normalization}. In particular, no two edges with a common endpoint cross. Form the blocks $J^{ik}$ of its signed-intersection matrix. Use the map $\Phi$ from Lemma~ef{lem:detector}, with any one tuple of distinct nodes, and set \[ R_{ik}=\Phi(J^{ik}),\qquad X_i=R_{i1},\qquad Y_k=R_{11}-R_{1k}. \] Lemma~ef{lem:additive} and the annihilation property of $\Phi$ imply  egin{equation} R_{ik}=X_i-Y_k. \end{equation} Thus the matrices have the difference form required by Corollary~ef{cor:rank-sum}. We next check its invertibility hypothesis on diagonal blocks and bound the other block ranks by crossings. All edges in the star at $a_i$ are oriented outward and do not cross one another. Consequently $J^{ii}$ is exactly half the sign matrix of the linear spoke order at $a_i$. Lemma~ef{lem:detector} gives  egin{equation} \mathrm{rank} R_{ii}=d\qquad(1\le i\le m). \end{equation} For $i
e k$, let $c_{ik}$ be the number of crossing points between edges incident with $a_i$ and edges incident with $a_k$. The entries $J^{ik}(p,p)$ may contain a local term at $b_p$, but $\Phi$ annihilates all diagonal entries: the factor $x_p-x_q$ in \eqref{eq:detector-definition} makes $B_{pp}=0$. If $p
e q$, the two edges $ip,kq$ have no common endpoint, so $J^{ik}(p,q)=I(ip,kq)$. Each nonzero such entry requires at least one crossing and contributes to $R_{ik}$ a matrix of rank at most one. Rank subadditivity yields  egin{equation} \mathrm{rank} R_{ik}\le c_{ik}\qquad(i
e k). \end{equation} This estimate counts crossing points correctly even when a pair of edges crosses repeatedly: cancellation in the signed sum can only reduce the number of nonzero contributions. Corollary~ef{cor:rank-sum}, applied to \eqref{eq:rank-family}--\eqref{eq:diagonal-ranks}, now gives \[ 2d_m d \le \sum_{i
e k}\mathrm{rank} R_{ik} \le \sum_{i
e k}c_{ik} =2c(D). \] The last equality holds because each crossing belongs to exactly two ordered pairs of distinct first-class stars. Thus $\mathrm{cr}(K_{m,n})\ge d_m d_n$ for odd $n\ge3$. \subsection{The even case} We use the vertex-deletion count appearing in Kleitman~\cite[Section~3, equations~(6)--(7)]{Kleitman1970} and Woodall~\cite[Theorem~1 and Corollary~1.1]{Woodall1993}. Let $n>2$ be even, and start again with a normalized minimum drawing $D$. Delete each of its $n$ second-class vertices in turn. Each remaining $K_{m,n-1}$ drawing has at least $d_m d_{n-1}$ crossings by the odd case. Since the two edges at any crossing have distinct second-class endpoints, that crossing remains in exactly $n-2$ of the deleted-vertex drawings. Therefore \[ (n-2)c(D)\ge n d_m d_{n-1}=(n-2)d_m d_n, \] where the last identity follows directly from \eqref{eq:dr} for even $n$. Division by $n-2$ and the upper bound \eqref{eq:upper} prove equality. Together with the zero-factor cases, this completes Theorem~ef{thm:main}. \qed

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma A.1
nodes.statement: \emph{Isolating the marked passages.} Call the vertices and crossing points of the given drawing its \emph{marks}. There are finitely many. Parameterize each edge injectively by $\gamma_e:[0,1]\to\mathbb R^2$. On each edge, choose pairwise disjoint parameter neighborhoods of its marked parameters, with disjoint closures, using one-sided neighborhoods at $0$ and $1$. For a mark $w$ on that edge, the image of the compact parameter set outside its chosen neighborhood avoids $w$, and hence has positive distance from $w$. If $w$ is not on the edge, the entire compact edge image has positive distance from $w$. Since all these conditions are finite, we may choose pairwise disjoint closed round disks $D_w$, centered at the marks, so that every visit of an edge to $D_w$ is in its prescribed parameter neighborhood, and nonincident edges avoid $D_w$ altogether. For an interior mark on $e$, remove the parameter interval from the first to the last visit to $D_w$. This removes the intervening excursions too. At the starting endpoint remove the interval through the last visit to its disk; at the terminal endpoint remove the interval from the first visit to its disk. These removed intervals are disjoint along each edge. The retained middle pieces are compact arcs with endpoints on disk boundaries and interiors in \[ \Omega=\mathbb R^2\setminus\bigcup_w D_w. \] They are pairwise disjoint, with distinct endpoints: every possible intersection in the original drawing was a mark and has been removed. This construction uses the first and last visits to each \emph{closed} disk, which exist by compactness. It does not require an arc to cross a round disk boundary only finitely many times. \emph{Replacing the exterior pieces.} The finitely many disjoint compact middle pieces admit pairwise disjoint open neighborhoods $U_P$. For a boundary endpoint $x$ of one piece $P$, take a short straight spur from $x$ radially outward from its disk. Its interior lies in $U_P\cap\Omega$. The spur tip can be connected to a nearby interior point of $P$ in that same open set. To see this directly, a sufficiently small exterior collar at $x$ lies in $U_P$ and meets no other disk. In polar coordinates about the disk center, choose the collar to have radius in $(r,r+\delta)$ and angle in a small open interval about the angle of $x$, where $r$ is the disk radius. It contains both the spur tip and all sufficiently nearby interior points of $P$. Radial paths and a short concentric arc connect those points inside the collar. Do this at both ends of $P$ and use the original middle subarc between the selected interior points. The resulting connection between the two spur tips lies in $U_P\cap\Omega$. Any continuous path with compact image in an open subset of the plane can be replaced, with the same endpoints, by a polygonal path in that open set: cover its image by small balls in the set, subdivide its parameter interval so each subarc lies in one such ball, and join successive subdivision points by straight segments there. Apply this to the connection just obtained, then attach the two spurs. If the result has loops, subdivide the finite union of its segments at all segment endpoints and intersections; for collinear overlaps, also subdivide at the overlap endpoints and identify coincident pieces. This is a finite embedded graph. A simple graph path between the original boundary endpoints is a simple polygonal arc, still in $U_P$ with its interior in $\Omega$. Carry out this construction for every $P$. Their disjoint neighborhoods ensure that no resulting exterior pieces meet. \emph{Filling the disks.} In a crossing disk join each of its two pairs of boundary endpoints by a straight chord. The four endpoints are distinct. The chords can therefore meet at most once, and any meeting is an interior transverse crossing: a line cannot contain four distinct points of a circle. In a vertex disk choose a new vertex point in its interior off the finitely many lines through pairs of its boundary endpoints, and join all the endpoints to it by straight spokes. These spokes meet only at the vertex. The new vertex points in different disks are distinct. Assemble the spokes, chords, and exterior polygonal pieces in their original edge order. Each resulting edge is simple: the exterior pieces are disjoint, the disks are disjoint, and an edge uses at most one chord or spoke in any one disk. Its interior avoids all vertices. Every inter-edge crossing lies in an original crossing disk, with at most one crossing in that disk and no third edge there. Thus the result is admissible, polygonal, and has no more crossings than the given drawing. It is straight near every vertex and every crossing. \emph{Removing adjacent-edge crossings.} Suppose two polygonal edges $e=vu$ and $f=vw$ sharing $v$ cross at $x$. As the graph is simple, $u\ne w$. Choose a small round disk about $x$ that meets only the two straight crossing strands and contains no other mark or bend. Swap the portions of $e$ and $f$ from $v$ up to this disk, then connect the swapped prefixes to the original suffixes. Inside the disk this pairs adjacent boundary endpoints, so two disjoint chords make the reconnections. The result is a walk from $v$ to $u$ and a walk from $v$ to $w$. The crossing at $x$ has disappeared. Outside the disk every old open track is assigned exactly once in total to the two new walks. The walks may have self-intersections.
